title: Stop reason
mindmap: Keep the loop going while stop_reason is "tool_use" and stop when it is "end_turn"; never stop because of the reply's wording or an iteration cap.
story: A waiter keeps going back to the kitchen while the customer is still ordering, and stops when the customer closes the menu. The waiter does not stop because the customer said "great" halfway through, and does not stop after exactly three trips. Claude's API tells your code the same thing in one field: stop_reason says whether Claude wants a tool run ("tool_use") or has finished its turn ("end_turn").
question: What does the code look at to decide whether to run another step: the stop_reason field, or something else?

signals.label: Words that point to reading stop_reason
words: decide when the agent is done

signals.label: Words that point to the trap
words: looks for phrases like "I have finished"

best: Send the request, look at stop_reason, run the tool and add its result to the conversation when it is "tool_use", and end the loop when it is "end_turn".

lookalikes.option: Stop when Claude's reply contains a phrase such as "task complete"
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works, but Claude's wording varies, so the loop sometimes stops mid-task or runs on; the field exists so you don't have to parse text.

lookalikes.option: Stop after a fixed number of iterations, such as 10
lookalikes.label: wrong primary stop
lookalikes.why: Works, but as the main stop it cuts off long tasks and wastes calls on short ones; a cap is only a safety net.

lookalikes.option: Stop as soon as the response includes any text
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works, but Claude often writes text and asks for a tool in the same response, so the loop ends before the tool runs.

lookalikes.option: Replace the loop with a fixed sequence of tool calls
lookalikes.label: different problem
lookalikes.why: Works, but it removes Claude's ability to choose the next step from what it just learned; it answers a design question, not a stopping one.

guideQuotes: Continue the loop when stop_reason == "tool_use"; terminate when "end_turn".
Anti-patterns: parsing natural-language signals to determine termination; arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stop; checking assistant text content as a completion indicator.
remember: The loop's stop sign is stop_reason: keep going on "tool_use", stop on "end_turn".

title: Coordinator split
mindmap: If whole topics are missing from the result and every subagent did its job, the coordinator split the task too narrowly, so fix the coordinator, not the subagents.
story: An editor asks three reporters to cover a town festival: one for food, one for music, one for parking. Each writes a great piece, yet the paper has nothing on the crafts fair. That gap is not the reporters' fault. Nobody was asked to cover it.
question: Did each subagent do what it was asked? If yes, the fault is upstream, in what the coordinator asked.

signals.label: Words that point to the coordinator
words: covers only part of the question

signals.label: Words that point to a subagent
words: results contradict the sources it was given

best: Widen the coordinator's decomposition so the subtasks cover the whole question, and give each subagent a brief with the goal and quality criteria.

lookalikes.option: Give the subagents better search terms or more sources
lookalikes.label: blaming the subagent
lookalikes.why: Works, but the subagents already did what they were asked; the missing topic was never in any Task prompt.

lookalikes.option: Add a gap check or reviewer after the report is written
lookalikes.label: too late
lookalikes.why: Works, but it pays for a wasted round and leaves the narrow split in place for the next run.

lookalikes.option: Run the subagents in parallel to finish faster
lookalikes.label: different problem
lookalikes.why: Works, but speed is not the problem; parallel calls cover the same narrow set of topics.

lookalikes.option: Give the coordinator a longer step-by-step procedure
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works, but coordinator prompts should state goals and quality criteria; more steps make the split more rigid, not wider.

guideQuotes: Coordinator handles task decomposition, delegation, aggregation, and selecting which subagents to invoke by query complexity.
Hub-and-spoke: coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, routing.
remember: When everyone did their part and something is still missing, look at who handed out the parts.

title: Subagent context
mindmap: A subagent knows only what its prompt tells it, so pass findings and sources explicitly, and launch parallel subagents as several Task calls in one response.
story: You hire a contractor to finish a room. They were not at last week's meetings, so they don't know the client hates grey. If you don't write it in their brief, they will paint it grey. A subagent is that contractor: it starts with an empty memory and sees only its Task prompt.
question: Was the fact the subagent got wrong actually in its Task prompt?

signals.label: Words that point to writing it into the Task prompt
Words that point to parallel Task calls

best: Write the complete earlier findings, the user's constraints and the source details (URLs, document names, page numbers) into each subagent's Task prompt, in a structured form; send independent subagents as several Task calls in one response.

lookalikes.option: Give the subagents shared memory or let them read the coordinator's history
lookalikes.label: doesn't exist
lookalikes.why: Works in other frameworks, but here subagents inherit nothing automatically; the prompt is the only channel.

lookalikes.option: Put the user's rules in the subagent's system prompt
lookalikes.label: wrong home
lookalikes.why: Works for rules that never change, but per-request facts like this user's constraints belong in the Task prompt for this request.

lookalikes.option: Summarise earlier findings in one short sentence to save tokens
lookalikes.label: loses information
lookalikes.why: Works, but the guide asks for complete prior findings; a one-line summary drops the numbers and the sources.

lookalikes.option: Let subagents talk to each other directly
lookalikes.label: wrong shape
lookalikes.why: Works in a mesh design, but the hub-and-spoke pattern keeps all communication going through the coordinator.

guideQuotes: Subagent context must be provided explicitly in the prompt (no automatic inheritance / shared memory).
spawn parallel subagents by emitting multiple Task calls in one response
remember: If it isn't in the Task prompt, the subagent doesn't know it.

title: Prompt or hook
mindmap: A rule that must hold every time, like verifying identity before a refund, goes in a hook or gate; a preference can stay in the prompt.
story: A shop can put a note by the till saying "offer the loyalty card", or it can build a till that won't open for a refund over $150 without a manager's key. The note works most of the time, and that's fine for a suggestion. The till lock works every time, and that's what money rules need.
question: If this goes wrong once, is that acceptable?

signals.label: Words that point to a hook or gate
Words that point to a prompt

best: Block the tool call in code until the condition is met (a PreToolUse hook or a prerequisite gate), and redirect to escalation when the policy says so.

lookalikes.option: Move the rule to the top of the system prompt and state it more firmly
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works, but prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate; a rule that must hold every time needs code.

lookalikes.option: Add few-shot examples showing the agent checking identity first
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works, but examples raise the rate without making it certain.

lookalikes.option: Use a PostToolUse hook to check the refund after it runs
lookalikes.label: too late
lookalikes.why: Works for cleaning results, but PostToolUse acts after the tool has run, so the refund has already happened.

lookalikes.option: Log every refund and review the log daily
lookalikes.label: too late
lookalikes.why: Works for audit, but logging prevents nothing.

guideQuotes: When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial ops), prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate.
Hooks give deterministic guarantees vs prompt-based probabilistic compliance.
remember: If once is too many, use code; if it's a preference, use the prompt.

title: Hook to clean up data
mindmap: Use a PostToolUse hook to tidy mixed formats, such as dates and status codes, before Claude sees the result, instead of asking Claude to do it.
story: Three suppliers send invoices: one writes dates as 03/04, one as 4 March, one as a number of seconds. A good office manager has the post room stamp every invoice with one date format before it reaches the accountant. The accountant never has to guess. A PostToolUse hook is that post room.
question: Is the problem in what the tool returns, and could plain code fix it the same way every time?

signals.label: Words that point to a PostToolUse hook
Words that point elsewhere
words: the agent calls the wrong tool
the rule must block an action

best: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts every tool result to one format (or removes a field) before Claude reads it.

lookalikes.option: Tell Claude in the system prompt how to read each format
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works most of the time, but Claude can still misread a timestamp; code converts it the same way every time.

lookalikes.option: Ask each team that owns a tool to change its output format
lookalikes.label: slow and out of your hands
lookalikes.why: Works eventually, but you don't control those tools, and the next new tool brings a new format.

lookalikes.option: Use a PreToolUse hook
lookalikes.label: wrong hook
lookalikes.why: Works for checking a call before it runs, but the mess is in the result, which PreToolUse never sees.

lookalikes.option: Add a separate normalising subagent
lookalikes.label: overbuilt
lookalikes.why: Works, but it adds a model call, cost and its own error rate for a job a few lines of code do exactly.

guideQuotes: PostToolUse hooks intercept results for transformation before the model sees them.
Normalize heterogeneous formats (Unix ts, ISO 8601, numeric codes); block policy-violating actions (e.g., refunds > $500) and redirect to escalation.
remember: Fix messy tool results in code on the way back, before Claude reads them.

title: Fixed chain or Claude decides
mindmap: If the steps are known in advance, use a fixed chain of prompts; let Claude choose the steps only when they depend on what is found along the way.
story: Baking a cake from a recipe is a fixed chain: mix, pour, bake, ice, the same every time. Finding out why the cake sank is different: what you check next depends on what you just found. Use a recipe for the first and a detective for the second.
question: Can you write down every step before you start, or does the next step depend on what you discover?

signals.label: Words that point to a fixed chain
Words that point to Claude deciding

best: For known steps, chain prompts: analyse each item on its own, then run one integration pass across them. For open problems, let Claude build its plan from what it discovers.

lookalikes.option: Give one agent everything and let it decide the steps
lookalikes.label: overbuilt
lookalikes.why: Works, but when the steps are known it adds unpredictability and cost for no gain.

lookalikes.option: Hard-code the investigation steps as a decision tree
lookalikes.label: too rigid
lookalikes.why: Works for cases you foresaw, but an open problem needs the next step chosen from what was just found.

lookalikes.option: Process all the files in one large prompt
lookalikes.label: attention dilution
lookalikes.why: Works for a few files, but quality drops as the prompt grows; per-file passes plus an integration pass keep it sharp.

guideQuotes: Fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) vs dynamic adaptive decomposition based on intermediate findings.
Prompt chaining: analyze each file individually, then a cross-file integration pass.
Adaptive investigation plans generate subtasks from what's discovered.
remember: Known steps get a recipe; unknown steps get a detective.

title: Resume, fork or start fresh
mindmap: Resume when nothing has changed, fork to try another approach from the same starting point, and start a new session with a summary when the earlier tool results are out of date.
story: You pick up a book where you left off when nobody has touched it. You photocopy a page to try two different notes on it. But if someone rewrote half the chapters while you were away, you don't trust your old bookmarks; you start from a fresh summary of what you know now.
question: Is what the old session saw still true, and do you want one path or two?

signals.label: Words that point to resume
words: pick up where it left off

signals.label: Words that point to fork
Words that point to a fresh session with a summary

best: Pick the one that matches: --resume for an unchanged task, fork_session for divergent approaches, or a new session seeded with a structured summary when the old tool results are stale. If you do resume after changes, tell the agent what changed.

lookalikes.option: Resume the old session after the files have changed
lookalikes.label: stale results
lookalikes.why: Works if you tell the agent what changed, but a fresh session with a structured summary is more reliable than old tool results.

lookalikes.option: Start every session from scratch
lookalikes.label: wastes work
lookalikes.why: Works, but it throws away valid context and repeats exploration when nothing has changed.

lookalikes.option: Run the second approach in the same session after the first
lookalikes.label: polluted context
lookalikes.why: Works, but the first attempt's reasoning colours the second; a fork gives each a clean branch.

guideQuotes: fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline.
Inform the agent about file changes when resuming after modifications.
Starting a new session with a structured summary is more reliable than resuming with stale tool results.
remember: Same world, resume; two paths, fork; changed world, start fresh with a summary.

title: Tool picker
mindmap: If Claude picks the wrong tool, first improve the tool descriptions (what each does, its inputs, its edge cases, when not to use it) before adding routers or new tools.
story: A new assistant has two folders labelled "Stuff" and "Things". They file papers in the wrong one, and it isn't their fault. Relabel them "Unpaid invoices" and "Signed contracts", with a note on each saying what does not go in, and the mistakes stop.
question: Does Claude have what it needs, in the descriptions, to tell these tools apart?

signals.label: Words that point to better descriptions
Words that point to something else
words: a prompt line ties a word to a tool
one generic tool does several jobs

best: Rewrite the descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases and boundaries ("not for X: use Y"). If a system-prompt line ties a keyword to a tool, remove it; if one tool does several jobs, split it.

lookalikes.option: Add a routing layer that picks the tool from keywords
lookalikes.label: overbuilt
lookalikes.why: Works on the cases it was written for, but it is more to build and maintain, can hide the right tool, and leaves the vague descriptions in place.

lookalikes.option: Add 5 to 8 few-shot examples showing which tool to call
lookalikes.label: later step
lookalikes.why: Works on cases like the examples, but it adds tokens to every call and leaves the cause in place.

lookalikes.option: Set tool_choice to "any"
lookalikes.label: different problem
lookalikes.why: Works to force a tool call, but it controls whether a tool is called, not which one Claude picks.

lookalikes.option: Merge the similar tools into one
lookalikes.label: wrong direction
lookalikes.why: Works to remove the choice, but the guide asks for purpose-specific tools with clear contracts, not a generic one.

guideQuotes: Include input formats, example queries, edge cases, boundaries.
Ambiguous/overlapping descriptions cause misrouting; keyword-sensitive system-prompt wording creates unintended tool associations.
remember: Fix the labels before you build a sorter.

title: Tool failure
mindmap: Return a structured error that says what failed and whether a retry can help; never return an empty success, a generic "failed" or a crash.
story: You send someone to the bank. If it's closed, you need to hear "it was closed, it opens at 9, I got the deposit slip". "It didn't work" is useless, "there's no money" is a lie, and quitting the whole errand list is worse.
question: After this failure, does the next decision-maker know what happened, what was tried and what is still usable?

signals.label: Words that point to a structured error
Words that point to the trap
words: returns an empty list on failure
raises an exception that ends the workflow

best: Return isError with the error category (transient, validation, business, permission), whether it is retryable, a plain description, the attempted query and any partial results. Retry short blips locally; never retry a business rule.

lookalikes.option: Return an empty result marked as success
lookalikes.label: inventing information
lookalikes.why: Works to keep the run going, but "we couldn't check" becomes "there is none", and the agent acts on it as fact.

lookalikes.option: Return a uniform "Operation failed" message
lookalikes.label: losing information
lookalikes.why: Works to signal failure, but the decider can't tell a timeout from a policy refusal.

lookalikes.option: Retry with backoff, then report "unavailable"
lookalikes.label: losing information
lookalikes.why: Works for a short blip, but a long outage still ends in a generic status, and retrying a policy refusal never helps.

lookalikes.option: Raise an exception to a top-level handler
lookalikes.label: over-terminating
lookalikes.why: Works to stop bad data, but one failure throws away all finished work and every chance to recover.

guideQuotes: Uniform "Operation failed" prevents good recovery decisions.
Distinguish transient (timeouts), validation (bad input), business (policy), permission errors.
Generic statuses hide context; silently suppressing errors or terminating on single failure are both anti-patterns.
remember: A failure should arrive with its name, its cause and what was saved.

title: Too many tools
mindmap: Give each agent the 4 or 5 tools its job needs, not all 18, with a small shared tool only for a need that comes up often.
story: A chef with a hundred gadgets on the counter spends time choosing and sometimes grabs the wrong one. A chef with the five knives the dish needs works fast and right. And the pastry chef shouldn't have the meat cleaver at all.
question: Does this agent really need every tool it has?

signals.label: Words that point to scoping the tool set
words: uses a tool outside its role
selection got worse after adding tools

signals.label: Words that point to a limited shared tool
words: keeps handing back to the coordinator for one lookup

best: Scope each agent's tools to its role, and give a narrow cross-role tool only for a frequent need instead of the whole set.

lookalikes.option: Improve all 18 tool descriptions
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works a little, but good descriptions don't fix the fact that 18 choices degrade selection.

lookalikes.option: Add a router agent that picks tools for the others
lookalikes.label: overbuilt
lookalikes.why: Works, but it adds a model call and a failure point when scoping the list fixes the cause.

lookalikes.option: Tell each agent in its prompt which tools not to use
lookalikes.label: only usually works
lookalikes.why: Works most of the time, but a tool the agent has is a tool it may misuse; remove it instead.

lookalikes.option: Give the subagent no cross-role tools, so it always asks the coordinator
lookalikes.label: too strict
lookalikes.why: Works, but for a frequent need the round trips add delay; a limited cross-role tool is the guide's answer.

guideQuotes: Too many tools (18 vs 4-5) degrades selection reliability.
Agents with off-specialization tools misuse them.
Scoped access; limited cross-role tools for high-frequency needs.
remember: Fewer, role-fitted tools beat more tools with better labels.
